subject: storytime
title: Millions of Cats
about: Wanda Gág's 1928 picture book about a lonely old man and woman, a hill covered with cats, and the one shy kitten who stays. First graders love the counting refrain of hundreds and thousands and millions of cats, and the ending is a kind one about being loved. In this softened telling the cats only quarrel and run off in a huff; it is a public-domain story retold in first-grade words, five pages long.
tip: Ask: why did the shy kitten stay when all the other cats ran away?

book.author: Wanda Gág (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: One old man, one hill, and millions of cats.

passage.text:
Once there was an old man and an old woman.
They lived in a neat little house.
They were happy.
But they were lonely.
"I wish we had a cat," said the old woman.
"I will find you one," said the old man.
So he set off over the hills.
***
At last he came to a hill.
The hill was covered with cats!
There were hundreds of cats.
There were thousands of cats.
There were millions of cats, all over the hill!
"Oh!" said the old man.
"Now I can pick the prettiest one."
He picked a white cat.
Then he saw a black cat.
He could not choose.
So he took them all.
***
The cats followed him home.
Hundreds of cats, thousands of cats, millions of cats!
The old woman came to the door.
"My dear!" she said.
"We cannot keep millions of cats."
"Let the cats pick," said the old man.
"Which cat is the prettiest?"
"I am!" said one cat.
"No, I am!" said another.
"I am the prettiest!" they all said.
***
The cats began to quarrel.
They hissed and fussed.
They stamped their paws.
Then, in a huff, they all ran away.
Hundreds and thousands and millions of cats, all gone!
The yard was quiet.
Only one little kitten was left.
She was thin and shy.
She had hidden in the tall grass.
"I did not think I was pretty," she said.
"So I did not quarrel."
***
The old man picked up the kitten.
The old woman gave her warm milk.
They loved her every day.
The kitten grew plump and happy.
Her fur shone like silk.
The old man smiled.
"She is the prettiest cat of all!"
"I think so, too," said the old woman.
A little love can make anyone shine.

cards.q: What did the old woman wish for?
cards.note: The old man and woman were happy but lonely, so she wished for a cat to keep them company.

cards.q: How many cats followed the old man home?
cards.note: Hundreds of cats, thousands of cats, millions of cats, all in a line behind him.

cards.q: What did the cats quarrel about?
cards.note: Every cat said I am the prettiest, and the fuss sent them all off in a huff.

cards.q: Which cat stayed with the old man and woman?
cards.note: She had hidden in the tall grass and did not quarrel, because she did not think she was pretty.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The old woman's wish is what sends the old man off over the hills.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Warm milk and love made the thin kitten plump, shiny and the prettiest cat of all.

cards.q: How did the old man and woman feel at the start?
cards.note: They were happy in their neat little house, but lonely, which is why they wanted a cat.
A little love can make anyone shine; the last line says it.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'quarrel' mean?
cards.note: To quarrel is to argue in an angry way, the way the cats did over who was prettiest.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.
